title: Deriving a Recurrence from the Code
quickIdea: Write what one activation costs and how many smaller activations it starts. That equation answers both the count question and the complexity question.
remember: Read the code as an equation: each branch of an if-chain is one line of the recurrence, and the base branch gives the boundary value.

GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.51: func(start, end) sets length = end+1-start and then maps length mod 3 to 0 -> length-1, 1 -> length-1 plus one, 2 -> length-2. The returned value is 1 exactly when the starting length is 1 mod 3 and 0 otherwise, so the maximum over all legal arguments is 1.

A recurrence for a call count keeps a +1 for every activation; a recurrence for time keeps the work done in one activation, which may be O(1) or O(n). Writing one and solving the other is the classic error.
When two parameters move at different rates the recurrence is two-dimensional. In GATE CSE 2018 Q.45 x halves (ten levels) while y decrements (1023 values), and the answer is the product 10 x 1023.

Once the recurrence is right, either tabulate it - small arguments, exam-friendly arithmetic - or solve it with substitution or a recursion tree. The Master theorem applies only to the divide-and-conquer shape T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).
Every GATE recursion question of the last five years is answered by one of three moves: trace the order, count the activations, or evaluate the recurrence bottom-up.

example.prompt: int func(int start, int end) { int length = end+1-start; if ((length<1) || (start<0) || (end<0)) return 0; if (length%3==0) return func(start+1, end); else if (length%3==1) return 1 + func(start, end-1); else return func(start+2, end); } What is the largest value func can return?
example.work: Write F(L) for the value when the length is L: F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(2) = F(0) = 0, F(3) = F(2) = 0, F(4) = 1 + F(3) = 1, F(5) = F(3) = 0, F(6) = F(5) = 0, F(7) = 1 + F(6) = 1. After a 1 is collected the length moves to a value that is 0 or 2 mod 3, so a second 1 is never collected.

gateAngle: 2026 Set 2 Q.51 is a recurrence question disguised as a trace: the three branches are three lines of a one-variable recurrence, and the answer follows from the table. Recognising that the length, not start or end, is the state is the whole difficulty.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.51: the maximum value returned by func.
variations.why: The single increment can be collected only once, because the branch after it changes the length mod 3 to 0 or 2.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For the same func, what does func(0, 0) return, and why?
variations.answer: 1: the length is 1, so the middle branch runs and returns 1 + func(0, -1), and that call returns 0 because end < 0.
variations.why: Shows that the base case can fire through the start < 0 or end < 0 test as well as through the length test.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does the call-count recurrence for GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.39 add 1 per activation while its time complexity is exponential?
variations.answer: Because the count and the cost measure different things. The count is the number of nodes in the call tree, which is 25 for n = 6; the cost is that same count multiplied by the constant work per activation, so both grow at the same rate here - exponential in n for large n.
variations.why: The two recurrences coincide for this function, which is why it is easy to confuse them; they diverge when one activation does O(n) work.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A function recurses on n-1 and n-2 and prints once per activation. Write its recurrence and give the value for n = 5.
variations.why: The same tabulation on the Fibonacci-shaped recurrence, which is the most likely twist on the 2015 question.

trap.what: Deriving the recurrence from the arguments as written rather than from the quantity the code actually recurses on.
trap.why: In 2026 Set 2 Q.51 the code passes start+1, end-1 or start+2, but the state that drives the recursion is the length end+1-start. A recurrence written in start and end is two-dimensional and hides the one-line pattern.
trap.counterexample: Writing F(start, end) for the 2026 Set 2 question gives three coupled branches; writing F(length) gives F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(2)=F(0), which solves it in four lines.

check.question: void p(int n) { if (n == 0) return; p(n-1); p(n-1); } Write the number of activations T(n) and give T(4).
check.explanation: Each level doubles the calls below it and adds itself: T(1) = 3, T(2) = 7, T(3) = 15, T(4) = 31, which is 2^(n+1) - 1.
